title: Reading the query plan and the bytes actually scanned

videos.script: Every query has two numbers you can know before it runs, and one you only learn after. {{three}} The first is the bytes it will be billed. That is fixed by the columns it names, the partitions it keeps and their types. {{fixed}} You will write that computation as a short program, a dry run you can read. {{program}} BigQuery's own dry run and maximum bytes billed do the same against the real table. They cannot run here, and you will see exactly how they are typed. {{dryrun}} The second is the plan. DuckDB prints its plan as a tree, with the rows and the time of every step. {{plan}} BigQuery's plan is a graph of stages across many slots, joined by the shuffle. You will learn to read it from Google's documentation. {{graph}} And then the bytes actually read. The district query would be billed fifteen megabytes, and reads three from disk. {{read}} Why the bill ignores compression is the last question. {{why}}
